title: Rava bar Sheva
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman calls him Ravina’s student. In the account at Shabbat 140a (cited by Hyman as 139b), he says, “I was standing before Ravina. It was stirred for him with a garlic stalk, and he ate it.”

In Berakhot 14a, Rav [Rava, according to Dikdukei Soferim] bar Sheva came to Ravina on a day when an individual does not recite the complete Hallel. Ravina did not interrupt for him, because Ravina did not regard Rava bar Sheva as sufficiently important.
Hyman says Seder HaDorot conflated him with Rav bar Sheva, who was a student of R’ Nachman.

notes.text: Hyman supplies Shabbat 139b; the matching garlic-stalk account is on 140a. The supplied לי suggests “for me,” while the checked text says ליה, “for him.” Berakhot 14a makes Ravina the one who did not regard the visitor as sufficiently important.

No new primary scalar was returned. The earlier recorded garlic-stalk comparison is Shabbat 140a beside supplied 139b, not a new whole-page inspection or proof that Hyman’s account begins on a page turn. Supplied לי, for me, remains against the earlier ליה, for him. Berakhot makes Ravina the one who did not regard the visitor as sufficiently important, not the reverse. Hyman’s Rav/Rava variant and accusation that Seder HaDorot conflated two figures remain attributed. The unmatched [1] and the abbreviated Nachman title are preserved without a new footnote or authority merge.

Hyman’s printed article (vol. III, p. 1061) gives Shabbat 139b and reads ליה, “for him,” as does the passage at Shabbat 140a:6. The supplied transcription has לי, “for me,” and an unmatched [1]. The Davidson translation leaves the stirrer unnamed. At Berakhot 14a the standard text has Rav bar Sheva. Dikdukei Soferim preserves a manuscript reading with Rava and an additional Rav before Sheva. Seder HaDorot explicitly assigns the Shabbat passage to Rav bar Sheva, the identification Hyman disputes.
